Les Montréalais racisés disent stop au p: Racialized Montrealers Say Stop to Racial Profiling by the SPVM
Deux rapports sur les interpellations po: Two reports on police stops and racial profiling in Montréal were presented to the Public Security Commission.

La semaine dernière, j’ai assisté à la p: Last week, I attended the public presentation of two reports commissioned by the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) on racial profiling in police stops. Community organizations, anti-racist activists and Montrealers had been eagerly awaiting this meeting, since the reports were published in 2023.
Il s’agit de deux documents très importa: These two documents are very important for racialized communities, because they scientifically establish the existence and scale of racial profiling by some police officers. The big surprise of the evening was the absence of SPVM representatives. Not a single officer from the metropolis’s police service came to hear the concerns and questions, whether from the research teams the SPVM itself had mandated or from the people in attendance.
Je vous propose de revenir tout d’abord: I suggest we begin by looking back at this meeting, which was marked by the emotion of victims of racial profiling. After that, you’ll find a summary of the main takeaways from these reports, which run to hundreds of pages.
<strong>Un an et demi après leur publica: A year and a half after they were published and handed over to the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM), two reports on police stops and racial profiling in Montréal were finally presented to the Public Security Commission at city hall on Wednesday, Dec. 11. The public presentation gave Montrealers a chance to voice their concerns and their hope of getting some answers. At the heart of this important discussion, however, the SPVM was conspicuous by its absence, leaving questions hanging and citizens angry. Report.
Alors que la lumière commence à baisser: As the light begins to fade and the rain turns icy, about thirty citizens crowd into city hall on this Wednesday, Dec. 11, at 3 p.m. Outside the door of the Salle des Armoiries, six police officers stand guard. Inside, the members of the Public Security Commission face the public and the researchers, who have the floor to present the two reports on racial profiling.
Au cours de cette rencontre publique, le: During the public meeting, the two groups of researchers presented eloquent findings that highlighted the scale of the phenomenon and the SPVM’s “lack of will” to truly tackle it. “Police stops are an undeniably discriminatory practice, and it isn’t getting any better,” says one of the researchers bluntly.
Le premier rapport, commandé par le SPVM: The first report, commissioned by the SPVM and the City of Montréal, was written by four academics: Victor Armony, professor of sociology at Université du Québec à Montréal; Alicia Boatswain-Kyte, assistant professor specializing in anti-Black racism at McGill University; Mariam Hassaoui, professor of sociology at TÉLUQ University; and Massimiliano Mulone, associate professor at the School of Criminology at Université de Montréal.
Ils ont analysé plus de 270 000 interpel: They analyzed more than 270,000 police stops made without cause in Montréal between 2014 and 2021, as well as interviews with 92 police officers. By the end of the report’s 296 pages, the scale of racial profiling by police officers in random stops in public space is impossible to ignore.
Le second rapport, présenté par une autr: The second report, presented by another independent research team, looks more specifically at traffic stops. It was also produced at the request of the SPVM and the City, by the Collectif de recherche sur les interceptions routières et le profilage racial, led by Marie-Eve Sylvestre. The study reveals an even more pronounced pattern of discrimination in SPVM traffic stops.
Cette présentation publique, réclamée pa: This public presentation, which community organizations have been demanding since the reports were published in 2023, was a chance for Montrealers to voice their concerns and get some answers. The SPVM, on the other hand, was conspicuous by its absence, and many did not hesitate to say so.
<strong>Des citoyens dénoncent l’absence: Citizens denounce the absence of any SPVM representative
Après une présentation détaillée de plus: After a detailed presentation of the research findings lasting more than two hours, the tension rises a notch in the Salle des Armoiries when the public question period begins.
« Je voulais absolument être présente po: “I absolutely wanted to be here to tell the SPVM all the harm they do to us, and to ask why it keeps going after so many years,” Nicole says with a sigh. Seated on one of the room’s wooden benches, the woman in her fifties says that one of her sons “was harassed by the police” when he was 15.
« J’habite à Saint-Léonard, on est origi: “I live in Saint-Léonard, we’re originally from Haiti; and the first time my son got a ticket from the police for crossing on a red light, my first reaction was to take the officers’ side. For me, respect is very important, and it’s central to how I was raised. If a teacher or anyone in authority says something, I’m going to back them up,” says the mother. “But the months went by, and he was getting stopped more and more often, with very borderline comments, racist remarks or insinuations, and that’s when I understood that he wasn’t the problem. We ended up driving him to school and picking him up every day because he was so stressed about making the trip alone.”
L’absence du SPVM cristallise des crispa: The SPVM’s absence crystallizes the tensions. To everyone’s surprise, no police representative was present at this presentation. The absence was widely pointed out by the research teams and by the citizens in attendance, as was that of the executive committee of the Public Security Commission.
« Je ne comprends pas que le directeur d: “I don’t understand why the police chief isn’t here tonight,” Nicole continues. “It’s such a lack of respect! I’m glad I saw the researchers’ presentation – it was incredible! – but I don’t see the point of asking questions to someone who isn’t here.” Bitter, she quietly leaves the room as soon as the research teams finish presenting the reports.
« Je trouve que c’est, une fois de plus,: “I think it’s, once again, a lack of consideration and proof that they don’t respect the racialized people of this city.” – Paul, a Montrealer
Quelques minutes plus tard, les citoyens: A few minutes later, the citizens present, including many activists, step up to the microphone one after another to ask their questions. In most cases, Daphney Colin, the Commission’s chair, gives the same answer: “This is for the SPVM, we will pass your question on to them.”
« Ça n’a aucun sens ! Pourquoi on nous f: “This makes no sense! Why bring us here if we can’t even talk to them? I think it’s once again a lack of consideration and proof that they don’t respect the racialized people of this city!” says Paul, a Montrealer outraged by this one-way exchange.
Sous un chapeau à bords larges, Anastasi: Under a wide-brimmed hat, Anastasia Marcelin, director of the Ligue des Noirs du Québec, nouvelle génération, is not backing down: “I became an activist because my brother was being harassed in Montréal-Nord, I had no choice. (...) Our communities contribute to Montréal’s development, this has to stop! The experts have said it, everyone has said it, we’re all here saying the same thing!” says the young woman before turning toward the glass door of the room. “The police officers out there, stop your racial profiling!” she shouts in their direction, making one of them smile.
Des applaudissements nourris laissent en: Sustained applause conveys the public’s frustration. Once again, she is given the same answer: “Your question, like all the others addressed to the SPVM, will be passed on to the SPVM.”
Les policiers à l'entrée de la salle ne: The police officers at the entrance to the room are hard to miss. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
« Madame la présidente, j’ai une dernièr: “Madam Chair, I have one last question,” ventures Mariam Hassaoui, one of the researchers and an author of the first report presented. “Is it usual to have this many police officers at the entrance to this kind of public meeting?” Murmurs ripple through the room. After a silence, the chair acknowledges that “it’s not really usual to have this many, but it seems the SPVM had information that there was a risk of a protest.” A sigh runs through the audience.
L’argument ne semble pas avoir convaincu: The argument doesn’t seem to have convinced the audience. “And they’re going to tell us they had to spend their time sitting across from us, looking at their phones and laughing, barely looking at us while we talk about them?” asks Redouane, a Montréal-Nord resident. “They couldn’t position themselves just a little farther away and act professionally, if they were really there to ensure our safety?” Redouane’s sarcastic tone makes no attempt to hide his bitterness.
Sur les bancs réservés au public, les vi: On the benches reserved for the public, faces are closed. Over the course of the testimonies, you can glimpse the wounds caused by racial profiling. The feeling of not belonging in Quebec society, the exhaustion of having to keep fighting, chronic anxiety – the consequences are many. All the more so because victims’ word is often called into question, as noted by Azzouz Abdellah, a community worker in Saint-Michel, who told La Converse about <l1>his experience of racial profiling</l1> last October.
Appelé au micro, un citoyen réclame une: Called to the microphone, a citizen demands support for victims. With an impeccably trimmed beard and a khaki shirt buttoned all the way up, Hamza Madani, who works at the Clinique juridique de Saint-Michel, has himself had the bitter experience of racial profiling. “I was getting stopped for no reason so often that I started making videos on YouTube and social media to denounce these practices. Today, in my work, I’m especially interested in police violence and I also co-host a podcast about it, because it’s time for this to stop,” the young man tells us.
Il s’adresse aux représentants de la Vil: He addresses the City’s representatives: “What do we do about the young people who have been through this kind of profiling? Who lost their girlfriend, their wife, their job, their employment, their income – all these consequences? Not everyone has a voice! There are young people who went silent (...), who drifted into crime or depression. What do you plan to do for them?” he asks.
La question de la prise en charge des vi: The question of support for victims came to the fore on Sept. 3, when the Superior Court of Quebec ordered the City of Montréal to <l1>compensate people who experienced racial profiling</l1>. That decision, however, applies only to police stops carried out between August 2017 and January 2019.
« Le policier a une arme à feu. Il peut: “The cop has a gun. He can do anything with it. A Black person’s word, well, it doesn’t count for much in the province we live in.” – Aiden
Les chercheurs du Collectif de recherche: The researchers from the Collectif de recherche sur les interceptions routières et le profilage racial met many victims who were left with both physical and psychological scars from these police practices. “I wanted to drop out of school, stop working; I had insomnia, I had so much rage, I wasn’t sleeping well [...] I could spend the whole night tossing and turning in my bed. Afterward, I didn’t understand how a human being can think he’s superior to another like that!” Aymeric told them. He suffered from severe headaches and insomnia after several stops.
D’autres vivent dans la peur et font de: Others live in fear and have recurring nightmares. “The cop has a gun. He can do anything with it. A Black person’s word, well, it doesn’t count for much in the province we live in,” says Aiden. Although the uniform is supposed to be reassuring, victims often say they have learned to fear it. “Some people are in constant hypervigilance when they walk down the street, or when they drive a car. They’ll count a full three seconds at every stop sign, drive more slowly… as if they had to be more perfect than everyone else so as not to get noticed,” says researcher Marie-Eve Sylvestre.
Les effets du profilage racial peuvent s: The effects of racial profiling can be felt in people’s finances and work lives. Beyond the fines to pay – which can add up to significant sums – repeated lateness, absenteeism and damage to one’s reputation can lead to losing a job. “I was a full-time student and I worked part-time with minimal hours, so it took my entire paycheque to pay it,” says Inès, a student who received a ticket she says was unjustified.
Enfin, la représentation des institution: Finally, how public institutions in general are perceived is also affected, according to the researchers. The feeling of being unable to get justice, of being excluded from Quebec society, or that police officers are allowed to disregard the law are impressions often reported by victims of racial profiling.
« J’ai de la misère à comprendre qu’il y: “I have a hard time understanding that there’s one justice for white people and another for Black people. Before, I didn’t see myself in a box; in my head, I wasn’t Black, I wasn’t white, I was someone, a human being who respects himself; but now, when I’m out on the street, it’s like I have a label on my forehead: ‘Ah, you’re Black!’ and they made me feel it all the time! It’s never home for me! And my kids who were born here, it’s as if they’re never fully Quebecers! I feel that stigma!” says Raymond.
Au-delà de la présentation des données d: Beyond presenting the data from their studies, the two research teams showed a united and determined front at the public meeting. All expressed their incomprehension at SPVM director Fady Dagher’s decision to refuse to implement their sole recommendation: an immediate moratorium on random police stops.
Pour Massimiliano Mulone, qui fait parti: For Massimiliano Mulone, who is part of the first research team, there should be no doubt: “We don’t agree with him when he says it would be a symbolic measure. It’s the opposite of a symbolic measure, since it’s very concrete! We don’t understand where that argument comes from…” the academic explains.
Les deux équipes de recherche lors de la: The two research teams during the presentation of the report. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
« Nous ne sommes pas contre l’idée du vi: “We’re not against the idea of the cultural shift* he talks about, but he himself says it will take several years. So what I say is, in the meantime, let’s put an end to this practice whose discriminatory nature is scientifically proven, and maybe in a few years we can bring it back. When you subject a population to discrimination, what you produce is not safety, but insecurity,” concludes Mulone, prompting a wave of applause.
Selon Alicia Boatswain-Kyte, qui a pris: According to Alicia Boatswain-Kyte, who took part in preparing the first report, the SPVM’s denial leads to “immobility” within the institution. “Since the majority of them don’t see themselves as racist and don’t see these behaviours in their colleagues, these accusations feel unfair to them. (...) The practices are not questioned, and no effort is made to change them,” she continues.
L’équipe de recherche espère également p: The research team also hopes to be able to consult the SPVM’s recent data. “The latest data the SPVM has provided on stops dates from 2021. We would like to know whether the SPVM will make the data for 2022, 2023 and 2024 public,” asks Victor Armony.
<strong>Les sept grands points de ces ra: The seven key points of these reports
<strong>Les personnes autochtones, noire: Indigenous, Black and Arab people are 2.6 to 6 times more likely than white people to be stopped for no reason.
En 2021, une personne autochtone courait: In 2021, an Indigenous person was 6 times more likely to be stopped by police than a white person. These are random stops, justified neither by any offence nor by reasonable suspicion or an ongoing investigation. That figure has nearly tripled since 2014.
Une personne noire courait quant à elle: A Black person was 3.47 times more likely to meet the same fate, and an Arab person 2.62 times more likely. Finally, Latino people are 1.26 times more likely to be stopped than white people.
<strong>Les jeunes hommes noirs et arabe: Young Black and Arab men are the most affected by racial profiling.
Les jeunes de 15 à 34 ans représentent e: Young people aged 15 to 34 account for about half of the people stopped by the SPVM each year. “Among the male population aged 15 to 34, more than a third of the people stopped in Montréal are Black, and one in six is Arab,” the researchers note. Being young thus increases the risk of racial profiling, which is already high for a racialized person.
Par ailleurs, si la proportion de jeunes: Moreover, while the proportion of young Black men who are victims of racial profiling has been relatively stable since 2014, that of young Arab men has risen sharply. In 2021, they accounted for nearly a quarter of all stops of young people. That is a disproportionate share, considering that people of all ages <l1>who identify as Arab make up only 8 per cent of Montréal’s total population</l1>.
« L’immense majorité des interpellations: “The vast majority of random stops are initiated by police officers themselves, rather than by reports from citizens,” explains sociologist Mariam Hassaoui, rejecting the argument that these biases are linked to 911 calls.
Un phénomène que les policiers expliquen: Police officers explain this by saying that racialized youth are supposedly more likely to commit offences. But here again, the numbers don’t match the theory.
<strong>Il n’existe pas de corrélation e: There is no correlation between ethnicity and criminality.
« Pour les policiers, c’est un profilage: “For police officers, it’s criminal profiling, not racial profiling,” the researcher reports. If the absence of a correlation between ethnicity and criminality had to be scientifically proven in order to try to put an end to this racist prejudice, well, this report has done it.
Les sociologues ont en effet utilisé l’I: The sociologists used the Index of over-stopping in relation to municipal bylaw offences (ISRI-RM) to demonstrate it. It involves comparing the number of stops targeting each racialized group with the number of offences committed by those same groups in Montréal. In a society without racial profiling, the former should be more or less proportional to the latter. But that is not the case.
Selon qu’il s’agisse d’infractions aux r: Depending on whether the offences are municipal bylaw violations or Criminal Code violations, the over-stopping rate for Black or Arab people varies between 20 per cent and 112 per cent. This proves that stops are “a stable and routine practice” that is “highly sensitive to prejudice” and leads to “racial profiling,” the researchers say.
L’équipe de recherche insiste sur le fai: The research team stresses that this is an “irrefutable” finding, which can therefore no longer be up for debate.
<strong>Le profilage racial est un phéno: Racial profiling is exacerbated on the road.
Derrière le volant, les personnes racisé: Behind the wheel, racialized people are more likely to be subjected to racial profiling during traffic stops.
Selon les chercheurs, les policiers moti: According to the researchers, police officers justify these stops with various reasons: windows tinted too dark, snow-covered plates, a “bandit-type” car, an evasive look, wearing a hoodie, having an Afro hairstyle, or driving a car that isn’t in one’s name. On this point, researcher Marie-Ève Sylvestre says wryly: “I’d like to say that I drive a car that’s in my husband’s name and I’ve never been stopped for that reason.”
Le rapport note que les contrôles peuven: The report notes that stops can quickly escalate, with “racial insults,” for example, once the person concerned asks questions about the reason for the stop or “has the misfortune of wanting their rights respected.” This can go as far as physical assault by police officers, the report points out.
En consultant les témoignages recueillis: Looking through the testimonies collected, we learn that some people are stopped from one to 10 times a month. One business owner even says he had his company’s name removed from his car so as not to get bad publicity from being seen pulled over by the police on the side of the road.
L’équipe de recherche a réalisé des entr: The research team conducted interviews with 92 Montréal police officers. An overwhelming majority of them believe racial profiling does not exist.
« Nous constatons qu’il existe, parmi le: “We find that there is widespread denial among law enforcement members of the problem of racial discrimination within their organization. Officers stress their commitment to serving and protecting all citizens, but also the fact that street checks are an essential practice. These practices are not being questioned, and no efforts are being made to change them,” says Mariam Hassaoui.
« L’interpellation aléatoire s’appuie en: “Random street checks rely largely on suspicion; so, it’s a practice characterized by its ambiguity (...) that follows a predictive logic, according to which, if a person catches our attention, it’s because they deserve it. It’s a practice that is particularly susceptible to prejudice and cognitive bias,” the researcher adds.
<strong>L’unique recommandation est d’in: The sole recommendation is to impose a moratorium on street checks.
« Nous avons proposé le moratoire de tou: “We proposed a moratorium on any police stop that is not based on the observation of an offence, reasonable suspicion or an ongoing procedure,” says Victor Armony. “Contrary to what has been said, this is our only recommendation in this second report.” It is a recommendation that SPVM director Fady Dagher already waved away when the report was released in June 2023.
Selon lui, un moratoire ne serait qu’une: According to him, a moratorium would be nothing more than a “symbolic measure” that would not “solve the problem at its source.” Yet in 2019, the first report, commissioned by the SPVM from the same researchers, was already alarming in this regard.
Fady Dagher avait alors annoncé la mise: Fady Dagher had then announced the introduction of a new street check policy. But having read the second report, it is clear that it has had no real effect on racial profiling, leaving racialized Montrealers to endure police discrimination just as before.
Interrogé par La Converse, le SPVM demeu: When questioned by La Converse, the SPVM remains evasive. “As an organization, we recognize the need to improve our practices. We remain committed to the steps undertaken since the first report we commissioned from the researchers, which was published in 2019,” the police institution assures us through its press office.
« Au cours de l’année 2025, le SPVM sera: “During 2025, the SPVM will be able to present the updated version of its policy on police stops, a policy it had initially rolled out in 2021.”
Aucun détail sur la façon dont cette « v: No details on how this “updated version” might prove more effective than the previous one.
